ECE 6612

Wi-Fi, DHCP and ARP trust

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a device establishing a radio link, obtaining network settings and resolving a local next hop.

A new laptop needs several pieces of information before it can load a page. Wi-Fi association establishes a local radio connection. Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, or DHCP, can assign the laptop an IP address, a DNS resolver and a default gateway. Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, maps an IPv4 next-hop address to a local media access control address, called a MAC address. Each stage has its own trust assumptions.

WPA2-Personal derives a pairwise master key from the shared password and network name. Its four-way handshake uses the client and access-point nonces and MAC addresses to derive pairwise keys and confirm possession. The resulting key material separates handshake confirmation, key protection and traffic protection. An observer with the shared password and the required captured handshake can derive that session’s pairwise keys. A weak password can also be tested against captured handshake evidence offline.

WPA2-Enterprise uses an authentication method through an authentication server rather than giving all users the same password-derived master key. For example, a correctly configured TLS-based EAP method validates the authentication server and establishes key material for the client’s association. Client certificate and server-name validation settings matter: accepting an impostor authentication server can expose credentials or permit an unintended connection, depending on the EAP method.

WPA3-Personal uses Simultaneous Authentication of Equals, or SAE, a password-authenticated key exchange. Its design resists the simple passive offline password test available from a WPA2-Personal handshake and supports forward secrecy for the established association. Security conclusions depend on the mode actually negotiated, including whether transition settings allow WPA2, and on implementation correctness. Radio encryption protects the client-to-access-point span; application protection continues independently beyond the access point.

DHCP discovery and offers commonly occur before the client has a trusted authenticated server relationship. A rogue local server can race a legitimate offer and supply an attacker-controlled DNS resolver or gateway. DHCP snooping constrains which switch ports may supply server messages. It can also build address bindings used by other controls. These defenses depend on correct switch configuration and trusted uplinks.

ARP announcements and replies similarly need an authenticated basis or enforcement policy. A local attacker can claim that a gateway IP belongs to the attacker’s MAC address, redirecting traffic through that device. Dynamic ARP inspection checks claims against permitted bindings, often learned through DHCP snooping; static mappings are another option in managed settings. End-to-end TLS still checks the intended server identity and protects records even when a local intermediary forwards the connection.

Example

A laptop uses gateway 192.0.2.1 in a teaching network. A rogue ARP reply maps that address to another local device’s MAC. Frames for the gateway then reach the rogue device, which may forward or drop them. Correctly authenticated TLS keeps the application’s encrypted contents protected across that forwarding path, while the attacker gains observation of traffic metadata and control over delivery.

Sources and scope
  • Course scope: Link Layer Security, including WPA2/3, Enterprise authentication, DHCP and ARP.
  • RFC 2131: DHCP.
  • RFC 826: ARP.
  • IEEE 802.11: RSN security, four-way handshake and SAE.
  • RFC 3748: EAP authentication framework.

Practice

1. A café gives every visitor the WPA2-Personal password. A visitor records another client’s complete required handshake. What information makes that client’s link keys derivable, and where does TLS protection end?

List the password-derived input and the public handshake inputs, then trace the two encryption spans.

The visitor has the shared password and network name plus captured nonces and client/AP MAC addresses, supplying the inputs for the WPA2-Personal pairwise derivation. This can expose that association’s link traffic under the stated capture and configuration assumptions. TLS continues from its client endpoint to its authenticated server endpoint, so properly protected application contents retain that separate end-to-end protection.

2. A new host accepts a rogue DHCP offer advertising an attacker-controlled resolver. The browser then reaches an impostor site address for a legitimate hostname. Which later check can detect that impostor?

Separate selecting an address from authenticating the named service.

TLS server authentication checks a valid certificate chain for the hostname the browser intended, along with handshake authentication. An attacker who only controls DHCP and DNS lacks the legitimate server’s required credentials, so normal validation rejects impersonation. The attacker can still disrupt delivery or observe traffic at its position.
